title: Research
text: My research uses applied microeconomics to study how producers respond to environmental risks and policy incentives. I examine how their decisions affect farm outcomes, public water systems, and downstream communities.

title: Research
text:
Working Papers

Agricultural Land Use and Nitrate in Public Drinking Water
How does farming affect the quality and cost of public drinking water, and who bears those costs? Using nitrate measurements from nearly 28,000 community water systems serving about 133 million people, we find that nitrate rises within weeks of rainfall in river-supplied systems with more upstream farmland. In systems that rely on wells, higher nitrate levels are associated with earlier agricultural land use. Existing agricultural land is associated with an estimated $102 million in annual water-supply costs across the systems included in the cost analysis. Groundwater systems serving fewer than 10,000 people account for 88 percent of the estimated groundwater costs. The findings can help agencies target conservation funding based on where communities get their drinking water.


The Heterogeneous Effects of Cover Crop Adoption on Prevented Planting Losses
This paper examines how the effects of cover crop adoption on prevented planting losses vary across regions, weather conditions, and cropping systems in the United States. Using data on cover crop adoption, producer-reported acreage, and local weather, we find that cover crops reduce losses in the Corn Belt, particularly during unusually wet planting seasons and in soybean production systems.


Tile Drainage and Downstream Flood Damages
Farmers install subsurface tile drains to remove excess water from fields and reduce crop losses. These investments can also change how quickly water reaches streams during heavy rainfall, with potential consequences for downstream communities. Using flood insurance claims from FEMA’s National Flood Insurance Program and data on heavy precipitation, we examine whether upstream tile drainage affects downstream flood damages. The findings can inform how drainage policy accounts for farm-level benefits and flood risk beyond the farm.

title: Mutahir Sultan
text:
About Me
I expect to earn my Ph.D. from Colorado State University in summer 2027. I earned my master’s degree in economics from the Institute of Business Administration in Karachi and my bachelor’s degree in economics from Quaid-i-Azam University in Islamabad.
At Colorado State, I worked on the Subsurface Irrigation Efficiency Project, an interdisciplinary study of irrigation management and water scarcity for corn and alfalfa producers in western Colorado.
